Work  /  15-40 Connection
Annual reports · Direct mail · Digital campaigns

Asking people to think about the thing they most avoid.

15-40 Connection teaches people how to catch cancer early. Two annual reports and three fall appeals, for a cause that has to raise money on a subject donors would rather not open.

Client

15-40 Connection

Role

Design, art direction and print production throughout; copy developed with the client

Years

2017, 2018, 2019

Mission

3 Steps Detect — early cancer detection education

The 2018 annual report. First responders on the cover, and a fire chief’s words instead of a mission statement.

The challenge

Cancer charities usually raise money for research or for treatment. Both come with a story a donor already understands — a patient, a trial, a cure to fund.

Education is harder to sell. There is no breakthrough to announce and no single person to save. What 15-40 Connection actually does is teach people to notice a change in their own body and act on it sooner. The benefit is invisible: the cancers caught early, in people who never knew how close they came.

The source material arrived unsorted. Leadership letters, program numbers, donor lists, survivor quotes, board bios, event photographs — all of it true, none of it in an order. Nothing could be laid out until someone decided what a donor reads first and what can wait.

The photography was the harder half. What existed was snapshots: events shot on phones, group photos in difficult light, almost nothing made for print. Every image that ran in these pieces was sourced, corrected and retouched first — a volume of work that is invisible when it goes well, and the only thing anyone notices when it does not.

Worse, the subject is one most people actively avoid. An appeal letter about cancer is a letter a donor is looking for a reason to put down.

The stakes, stated once, early, and without decoration.
The worst cancer diagnosis is a late one. Detect it early. A few seconds of reading time at highway speed, and the whole argument fits.

The approach

Find the order before the layout. The first pass was editorial, not visual — sorting what arrived into a sequence a reader could follow. What leads, what supports, what belongs at the back. The design decisions only got simple once that was settled.

Open with agency, not fear. The outer envelope carried five words: “Luck is not a strategy to beat cancer.” It concedes what the reader already suspects — that survival feels like chance — and immediately offers the alternative. Nothing to dread, and a reason to open it.

Let the person with the stake make the claim. The digital campaign is a mother, a Polaroid, and her own handwriting: “15-40 Connection Saved My Son!” — Love this kid!! No statistic outperforms a parent saying that sentence.

Write it so it survives a glance. The vehicle line — The worst cancer diagnosis is a late one. Detect it early. — came out of working on the copy alongside the client. Direct, simple, nothing to decode. A truck at highway speed gets a few seconds, and the whole argument had to fit inside them.

Make the arithmetic undeniable. Inside the report, a survival-rate table sets early detection against late detection, cancer by cancer. It is the entire argument for the organization, and it needed no adjectives — only clear rows.

The 2019 package. The line works before anything is opened; the reply card carries gift tiers, honor and memory giving, and matching gifts without crowding.
Every piece a donor touches, in the order they touch it. The reply card is shown as a production mechanical — type specs and all.

One idea, every format

The digital campaign ran across banner sizes with the composition rebuilt for each — not scaled. The Polaroid moves side to side, the headline reflows, and the claim stays first in the reading order at every ratio.

Three ratios, one hierarchy. Nothing is a squeezed version of anything else.

Off the page

The same argument had to work on a wall and on a race bib. A firehouse poster pairs Detect cancer early with the two-week rule; the Lisa Kaplan 5K carries a memorial fund into the organization’s mission without either one diluting the other.

Poster, race flyer, registration card. The hierarchy survives the change of medium.

Inside the reports

Two annual reports carrying the same job at length: leadership letters, financials as plain donut charts, and an impact spread built around the three steps rather than around the organization.

Impact, education in action, and the financials — the three spreads a donor actually reads before deciding.
The whole book — cover, letter, board, financials, impact, and six pages of donors who each had to find their own name.

The outcome

The organization reported 110,000 people taught 3 Steps Detect and 94% more education programs delivered in the year of the 2018 report, alongside its first national Audesse Award from the Massachusetts Society of Clinical Oncologists.

In 2021 — after this work — 15-40 Connection became DetecTogether, dropping the age range from the name to serve every age. The organization had outgrown the boundary it was founded inside. These were the pieces that made its case and asked for the money across the three years it took to get there.
